title: Preparing for winter: rising bills and homes left cold
label: 18 November 2026 · Winter energy bills
summary: The committee heard that a predicted rise in energy prices could leave households struggling with bills and debt, particularly renters in poorly insulated homes. A campaigner described serious damage from home upgrades carried out under ECO4 and the difficulty of getting repairs. The energy regulator, ombudsman and Minister discussed who was responsible, what help is available this winter, and how future upgrades might avoid the same failures.

The regulator that sets rules for Great Britain's gas and electricity companies.
An energy performance certificate that grades a property's expected energy efficiency from A, the best, to G, the worst.
A Government-backed discount on eligible households' electricity bills.
A scheme that required energy suppliers to fund home energy-saving improvements, particularly for eligible households.

chapters.title: What higher bills mean
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses warned that the predicted winter price rise would hit households already struggling with debt, rent and heating costs.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: A forecast today suggests the price cap could rise by 26%. What would that mean for families?

evidence.quote: Cornwall Insight is predicting that the price cap could rise by 26%, which is a significant increase on its previous estimate.
What does the increase in cost mean for families, quite apart from what Katie was saying there?

turns.speaker: Alex Belsham-Harris
turns.text: We expect households to pay around £200 more for energy from January to March than they did a year earlier. Among people coming to Citizens Advice with debt, average energy debt is over £2,000. Even after our help, more than half still can't cover essentials. The Government's £100 rebate will help some people, but it won't be nearly enough for those struggling most.

evidence.quote: we anticipate that it will mean people paying around £200 more on energy between January and March next year compared with what they were paying a year ago.
we are now supporting people with an average debt of over £10,000 and an average energy debt of over £2,000.
over half of those households still do not have enough money to cover their essentials.
we are concerned that, for people who are struggling most, that will not be anywhere near enough

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Will the planned scheme to clear some energy debt make a difference?

evidence.quote: what is your view of the Ofgem debt relief scheme? How effective is it going to be?

turns.speaker: Alex Belsham-Harris
turns.text: It's good that the scheme is going ahead and that pensioners and disabled people may qualify alongside people on income-related benefits. But it covers debt from 2022 to 2024. People have kept building up debt since then. If it clears only a small part of what someone owes, they may be less willing to engage with a repayment plan. We need the details.

evidence.quote: It is really positive that at the Budget the Government announced that the debt relief scheme will go ahead.
The debts that are eligible are from 2022 to 2024, and lots of people will have continued to build up significant debts from that point onwards
The benefit of the scheme should be to re-engage people, help them set up a repayment plan
it is not just households on means-tested benefits, but pensioners and people with disabilities.

turns.speaker: Nye Jones
turns.text: Renters face high rents and often live in homes that cost more to heat. On average, they spend 36% of their income on rent, and nearly half of rented homes in England fall below EPC C. Our estimates suggest that a recent price rise costs a family in an EPC D home around £180 a year, rather than the £60 increase Ofgem gave for a typical household.

evidence.quote: renters on average spend 36% of our income on rent
49% of rented homes in England are below EPC C
Ofgem estimated the annual household fuel bill increase would be £60, but our modelling found that, for a family living in an EPC D, it will actually be around £180

turns.speaker: Nye Jones
turns.text: The £100 rebate is poorly targeted for renters in house shares: a home's council tax band may say little about the incomes of the people living there. I'd expand the warm home discount and look at whether a home is expensive to heat, as well as the occupants' income.

evidence.quote: We feel like the £100 rebate was poorly targeted. Council tax bands were set in 1991 and there will be a lot of private renters who should receive it who will not, particularly those in house shares in cities
Expanding it, and looking particularly at homes with an EPC below C, would be a really good start.
There is a need to understand the whole picture, rather than just looking at someone’s income.

turns.speaker: Mike Reader
turns.text: Have things got better for people struggling to heat their homes since the election?

evidence.quote: Since the election, have things got better for those people who were struggling to heat their homes?

turns.speaker: Alex Belsham-Harris
turns.text: Not in many of the cases we're seeing. More people now get the warm home discount, and moving some costs off bills has helped some households. But because the discount is funded through bills, its net value fell for some recipients. Higher wholesale gas costs have also overwhelmed much of the help.

evidence.quote: Based on the client data and the people we are supporting at Citizens Advice, in many areas that is not the case.
because that is funded through bills, it also meant that the net benefit of the support reduced for everyone who received it
We have seen the positive action to take some of the levy costs off bills
a lot of these measures have been completely swallowed up by the massive increase in wholesale gas costs

turns.speaker: Nye Jones
turns.text: Renters have gained some security from the Renters’ Rights Act, but their finances have probably worsened. Rents have risen while the amount of housing support used to help pay private rent has stayed frozen. Nearly 60% of renters receiving that support now face a gap between their rent and the help they get.

evidence.quote: We saw the passing and implementation of the Renters’ Rights Act in May. That has been a major change that has redressed the power imbalance somewhat between tenants and landlords

There is the continued freeze of local housing allowance, for example. Rents have risen by 23% since it was last uplifted. Nearly 60% of renters who receive housing benefit or the housing element of universal credit have a shortfall between their rent and what they receive.
renters feel more secure, but probably have less money in their back pocket.

chapters.title: Warmer homes, without higher rent
chapters.takeaway: Better insulation could lower renters' bills, but witnesses wanted tenants to understand upgrades and keep the savings.

turns.speaker: Nye Jones
turns.text: The rule that will require most private rented homes to reach EPC C by 2030 is a better long-term answer: better-insulated homes cost less to heat. But the deadline was pushed back, the maximum landlords are expected to spend was cut, and we're concerned landlords could raise rents after upgrading a home.

evidence.quote: From 2030, all private rented homes, unless they have certain exemptions, will need to be at EPC C, up from EPC E. This is a much better longer-term solution to reduce fuel poverty among renters and make homes cheaper to heat.
The cost cap that sets the maximum that a landlord can spend was reduced from £15,000 to £10,000. We also saw the timeline put back.
We are also concerned in that regard about the prospect of landlords hiking the rent after investing to retrofit homes

turns.speaker: Graeme Downie
turns.text: Tenants often have little say over the heating system their landlord installs. How much does that matter?

evidence.quote: a tenant in fuel poverty usually has little or no say in what technology is used in their home. It is based on whatever the landlord has installed. How much impact does the heating system itself have

turns.speaker: Nye Jones
turns.text: All-electric homes are more expensive to heat, but insulation is the bigger issue for many renters. Poorly insulated homes lose heat, and tenants can't make major improvements themselves. Advice could help landlords choose the right work and explain it to tenants; existing grants could also help eligible homes sooner than 2030.

evidence.quote: Any home that is electric only is far more expensive to heat. It is around 2.5 times more expensive.
The big issue for rented households, though, as I said before, is the overall energy efficiency rating, particularly in terms of insulation.
the warm homes local grant already exists, which can fund retrofit improvements where tenants are on low incomes.
The Warm Homes Agency will play a critical role in making sure landlords take the right form of action for a home.

turns.speaker: Nye Jones
turns.text: The tenant needs to know what's being done and why. I'd prefer no rent rise after an upgrade. At the very least, a rise shouldn't wipe out the saving on energy bills: the point is to reduce hardship, not increase rent.

evidence.quote: It is important that the tenant understands the work that is being done and why, and the potential benefit.
We would prefer no rent increase.
it should not cancel out the bill savings. This policy is about fuel poverty; it is not about bringing rents up.

turns.speaker: Alex Belsham-Harris
turns.text: Installers should explain new heating systems clearly, and people should be able to get independent advice on whether a system suits them and how to use it. That matters especially in rented homes, where the landlord pays for the installation but the tenant lives with it.

evidence.quote: clear information from the installer is a vital part of that, and then access to independent advice about how to use these things efficiently and decide whether they are right for you in the first place.
the person paying for the installation and the person living with it are different.

chapters.title: When an upgrade goes wrong
chapters.takeaway: Dr Barrett described damaged homes and a difficult complaints process; other witnesses called for clearer routes to repairs.

turns.speaker: Dr Barrett
turns.text: I'm an ECO4 victim, and I campaign with others affected by the scheme. We estimate that more than 100,000 homes have been damaged. As far as I'm aware, none in our group has been properly repaired. Some people have badly installed insulation and heat pumps that can't heat their homes; they're going into another winter in cold, damp conditions.

evidence.quote: I am a victim of the ECO4 scheme and am here as a member of Fuel Poverty Action.
We estimate that there are over 100,000 houses that have been damaged by the ECO4 thing. As far as I am aware, none of them has been properly remediated, and certainly none in our group has.
There are people who have heat pumps that do not work and do not heat their houses because the insulation was done so poorly
lots of people are going into their third or fourth winter with wet, mouldy, cold homes that they cannot heat

turns.speaker: Claire Young
turns.text: Do you think the Government has a long-term answer to fuel poverty, or is it offering temporary help each winter?

evidence.quote: Do you believe that the Government have a strategy to address fuel poverty in the long term, or do you think they are simply applying a sticking plaster each winter?

turns.speaker: Dr Barrett
turns.text: Temporary help isn't enough. In my home, installers covered wet, mouldy walls with insulation. I've given Ofgem evidence that I believe shows fraud by the installer, but I haven't had a response. The company has since gone into liquidation. People need their homes repaired, and someone needs to be accountable when an installer disappears.

evidence.quote: I have so much evidence of fraud. I have photographs of things that never existed that it said were there.
I presented all that to Ofgem months ago and have not had any kind of response back.
This company has gone into liquidation.
In my house, they put insulation over wet, mouldy walls.

turns.speaker: Torcuil Crichton
turns.text: It sounds as though both the installation and the system meant to protect customers failed. How?

evidence.quote: It is not just that the installation broke; the system to protect consumers broke as well, didn’t it?
Tell us how.

turns.speaker: Dr Barrett
turns.text: When a company loses its approval or closes, people can be told the body overseeing it can't help. Complaints to different bodies can take months without getting the home fixed. We brought 10 cases to the Minister in June involving people who had followed the complaints process; none had been repaired when I gave evidence.

evidence.quote: It took six months with NAPIT and then it said, “There is nothing we can do. We have removed their accreditation, so we cannot do anything now.” TrustMark did not reply for a whole year
We presented 10 test cases to Martin McCluskey in June
Not one of those 10 test cases—sorry, migraine brain struggling to do words—has been remediated.

turns.speaker: Alex Belsham-Harris
turns.text: We've seen similar cases of poor home improvements. Future schemes need simpler protections: a clear way for people to get problems put right and stronger action against poor work. Those changes need to arrive quickly enough to protect people getting the next round of upgrades.

evidence.quote: reflects similar cases that we have seen at Citizens Advice, where people have had poor experiences of energy-efficiency installation.
replacing some of the patchwork of protections that currently exist and giving much clearer access to redress and much clearer and stronger enforcement.
We need to see that come in quite quickly if it is going to be aligned with the delivery of the next element of the warm homes plan

chapters.title: Who takes responsibility?
chapters.takeaway: Ofgem described a narrow role in ECO4, while the Minister acknowledged wider failures and disputed the campaigner's estimate of affected homes.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Ofgem was repeatedly mentioned in the evidence about ECO4. What was your responsibility when the work went wrong?

evidence.quote: There was plenty of reference to Ofgem in the last session.
What is Ofgem’s role with the response to the failings of ECO4?

turns.speaker: Neil Kenward
turns.text: The Government designed ECO4. Ofgem checked whether energy suppliers delivered the required number of improvements; checking their quality wasn't formally our job. The Government and TrustMark lead the programme to find and repair faulty work. We set up a contact centre and carried out or supported checks, but I recognise that repairs are moving more slowly than we'd want.

evidence.quote: The role of DESNZ is one of policy. It determines the programme of ECO4. We are the administrators of the programme. We check that the obligations on suppliers to deliver a certain number of interventions are met. Then the quality assurance around those, I believe, sits with TrustMark.
That is not formally our role.
We set up a dedicated call centre that still operates.
I recognise that the process is going slower than we would all want.

We do not have a formal role in the find and fix programme. We are supporting with advice and with the contact centre. We ran our own audit. Obviously, we supported and oversaw the audits by TrustMark.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Ed, people with failed installations may come to the Energy Ombudsman. Can you help them?

evidence.quote: Do you think it is an area that you should cover?

turns.speaker: Ed Dodman
turns.text: We can help with an energy-supply complaint, but not with a fault in the installed technology. People often can't tell which has caused their problem, so it's hard to turn them away. We support making complaints simpler and think we could help resolve some installation disputes.

evidence.quote: We support the idea of a warm homes ombudsman. That of course covers only publicly funded installations and improvements.
We could play a role in providing dispute resolution for consumers in some of these situations.

If it is a problem with the energy supply, we can help today, but of course the consumer does not know that. If it turns out to be a problem with their technology, unfortunately that does not fall within our remit.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Minister, Dr Barrett estimates more than 100,000 homes have been damaged. What has actually been found and fixed?

evidence.quote: the fact that 100,000 people are still suffering the consequences of poorly installed measures
We heard a figure of 100,000 people affected; that is a big gap with any of those figures.

turns.speaker: Martin McCluskey
turns.text: The figure of 100,000 isn't one I'd recognise. Our specific commitment covers 24,600 homes with problems involving solid-wall insulation, particularly outside walls. Ofgem has written to all of them. TrustMark has contacted 19,216 people, 11,141 checks have been completed and 2,227 repairs have been completed. About 4,000 people haven't been reached.

evidence.quote: I myself would not recognise the figure of 100,000, but we are obviously aware of other cases within ECO where there is remediation required.
There were 24,600 in that population that we were looking to remediate. So far, every property in that population has been contacted by Ofgem.
TrustMark has contacted 19,216 people. We have completed 11,141 audits, and we have completed 2,227 remediations on that population.
There are about 4,000 people in that population who we have not been able to contact.
the problems with solid wall insulation, particularly external wall insulation

turns.speaker: Martin McCluskey
turns.text: Other ECO4 cases also need attention. We've set up a team to help with especially complicated cases and a fund expected to cover about 170 cases where other ways to get repairs have failed. We've stopped new ECO4 installations because the scheme lacked proper oversight, and we're preparing new consumer protections.

evidence.quote: There will be a population of people who are not covered by the specific find and fix measures that we have set out who will require remediation
we have already set up a complex cases unit within the Department that is looking at some of the most complex cases.
We have enough funding in that for about 170 cases to be covered
we are no longer fitting new measures under ECO4. The scheme had clearly failed. It did not have correct oversight.
We consulted from June to September on a new model of consumer protection.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Why was poor work allowed to happen on such a scale?

evidence.quote: Why was this allowed to become such a massive problem?

turns.speaker: David Thomas
turns.text: The Department took its eye off the ball. The system didn't make clear who was overseeing whom or responsible for the work, and its checks weren't adequate. The most important lesson for the replacement system is to make those responsibilities clear.

evidence.quote: the Department took its eye off the ball. We did not set up a system that had clear enough accountability
there was a lack of clarity and accountability. Who was overseeing who? Who was responsible for the work?
The single most important thing we need to do in setting up the new consumer protection framework is to ensure that there is not that lack of clarity going forward.

turns.speaker: Mike Reader
turns.text: Did Ofgem fail, and what will change if it helps run future schemes?

evidence.quote: Would you accept that Ofgem failed here? What changes have you asked for from Ofgem to make sure that, if it has a role in administering future schemes, we do not see this happen again?

turns.speaker: Martin McCluskey
turns.text: There have clearly been failures in Ofgem and elsewhere. We're designing new consumer protections, but I can't set out their final form yet. If people are still being sent between Ofgem and the Department without help, I want to hear about it; that shouldn't be happening.

evidence.quote: There have clearly been failures in Ofgem. There have been failures in other parts of the system.
We are in the process at the moment of putting together the Government response, and I hope to have that out soon.
It should not be happening. That is the reason why the complex cases system was established, because people were being sent from pillar to post.
if that is still happening now I want to hear about it

chapters.title: Debt, billing and this winter's support
chapters.takeaway: Officials set out help already announced, but witnesses questioned whether it reaches the right people or prevents further debt.

turns.speaker: Mike Reader
turns.text: How much do households owe on energy bills, and will the debt plan bring it down?

evidence.quote: could you remind us of the current level of consumer fuel debt in the UK?
Do you think the Government have a coherent strategy to pay off that debt?

turns.speaker: Neil Kenward
turns.text: Bills unpaid for more than 91 days now total over £5 billion, about three times the level at the start of the decade. The plan combines debt relief, affordable repayment plans and changes to stop debts building up. I'm confident it will reduce debt over time, but higher bills mean debt is likely to rise this winter first.

evidence.quote: Ofgem measures it as unpaid bills after 91 days or more, and under that measure it is now over £5 billion.
The debt relief scheme is now moving ahead, as we have heard. Repayment is to try to ensure that customers are helped on to sustainable repayment plans
Reform is to make sure that the rules are suitable and to minimise the risks of debt accumulating
I am confident that this package of measures will substantially reduce energy debt over time.
in the short run, as energy bills go up, inevitably we are likely to see energy debt increase this winter

turns.speaker: Torcuil Crichton
turns.text: What problems most often bring customers to you, and can complaints be resolved sooner?

evidence.quote: what is the commonest thing that goes wrong and what are the quickest fixes?
Could that be tightened or shortened?

turns.speaker: Alex Belsham-Harris
turns.text: Affordability and incorrect bills are the main issues we see. Letting customers take an unresolved complaint to the Energy Ombudsman after six weeks, rather than waiting longer, strikes a reasonable balance. People who need more time or help must still get it. We'd also like prompt compensation when a faulty smart meter causes billing problems.

evidence.quote: The most common issues that we are seeing at the moment at Citizens Advice through our consumer service helpline, which is our specialist energy service, are around energy affordability and billing.
moving to a six-week wait before you can take your case to the ombudsman—we think achieve the right balance
We want to make sure that people who need more time are not feeling rushed through the processes
Ofgem has developed a guaranteed standard but not implemented it yet. We want to see that implemented as soon as possible. That would give people compensation if their smart meter is broken.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Minister, the witnesses say the £100 rebate won't cover the expected rise and may miss renters in shared homes. What's your response?

evidence.quote: the average bill will be £200 higher between January and March 2027 than it was in 2026, and that the £100 is not targeted, especially for those people in private rented accommodation, in particular those in shared properties.

turns.speaker: Martin McCluskey
turns.text: I won't pretend the support removes everyone's pressure. We've taken some costs off bills, extended the £150 warm home discount to 6 million households and announced £100 for homes in council tax bands A to D. There's no perfect way to reach everyone. We chose a broad payment reaching 20 million households alongside more targeted help, and we'll keep it under review.

evidence.quote: We ended ECO. That took money off bills. We now have the warm home discount, with a £150 discount extended to 6 million households
the £100 support for those people in council tax bands A to D.
I am not going to sit here and pretend that that is going to alleviate for everyone the pressure that will be felt over this winter
there is no perfect way to reach exactly the cohort that you want to reach. The judgment that we took was that reaching 20 million households
It is obviously something we will continue to keep under review.

turns.speaker: Ben Golding
turns.text: We'd target help more accurately if we knew each household's total income. Government records often show individuals' earnings, but not who lives together. We're testing how to bring different records together and connect them to energy bills. We wanted to use that approach this winter, but it isn't ready.

evidence.quote: Household income would be the best thing we could use to get closest to vulnerable households.
It is often very difficult to move from individual income to household income because HMRC will not necessarily know, for instance, who lives in a particular household.

bring those sources together and explore how we can use quite an innovative set of approaches to work out who is in a household, what the overall income at that household is, and then match that in turn to things such as energy bill meter references.
we would have loved to be able to use that this winter. It is not ready yet

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If the fixed daily gas standing charge is moved into the price of each unit used, won't people who need a lot of heat risk paying more?

evidence.quote: We heard about the impact of removing the gas standing charge and identifying the challenges for some families with children and people with disabilities in particular, but not exclusively. Is there additional support in place for them, because they will see their bills rise

turns.speaker: Martin McCluskey
turns.text: Without extra protection, our analysis says 60% of people would pay less, but others would pay more. We're examining what help people with disabilities, health conditions or medical devices might need. We haven't settled that yet.

evidence.quote: we recognised that, as soon as you move to more emphasis on the unit rate, there are potential impacts
We are going to look in detail at that and at what might be required as part of the work that we are doing on the removal of the gas standing charge.
disabled people or those who rely on medical devices having to pay significantly more.
without any mitigation, 60% of people would be better off

turns.speaker: Melanie Onn
turns.text: The current definition of fuel poverty counts people only if they're on a very low income and live in a poorly rated home. Does that really capture everyone who can't afford to keep warm? And how long will people have to wait for better homes rather than another payment?

evidence.quote: Does the definition of fuel poverty meet current expectations of what we would generally understand to be fuel poverty?
It is very low.
For how long are we going to keep just giving people money to try to keep themselves warm through cold periods?
How long do people have to wait for?

turns.speaker: Martin McCluskey
turns.text: We are looking at whether the definition reflects people's experience and have added a separate measure of whether energy is affordable. Home upgrades are happening now, though there's a limit to how many the Government can fund each year. We aim for 5 million upgrades by 2030; much of that depends on new requirements for rented homes, not just Government-funded work.

evidence.quote: we have already committed that we are going to look, through this Parliament, at potentially setting up a new definition of fuel poverty.
I was very keen that we did not have just the LILEE measure within the fuel poverty strategy, but also an affordability measure.
There is a limit to how much we can deliver each year, because of finances, but we are delivering tens of thousands of home upgrades to people right now
The 2030 target is 5 million home upgrades. As I was saying in response to Claire’s question earlier, it is a mixture of the change in regulation and the Government schemes.

the biggest step forward that we are going to have in terms of upgrading people’s homes is through the regulatory changes that we have made, particularly on minimum energy efficiency standards in the private rental sector
